statement: In dried cannabis flower that licensed growers sent for state compliance testing to six commercial laboratories in six US states (Alaska, California, Florida, Michigan, Oregon and Washington; December 2013 to January 2021; 89,923 samples after cleaning, 42,843 with terpene results), the Indica, Hybrid or Sativa category that one consumer cannabis website's strain database links to each strain name, matched by name to the growers' own sample names (so the category is the website's, not necessarily what each package said; 73.4% of samples could be given one), was barely related to the samples' terpene profiles, the mix of the compounds the authors describe as responsible for cannabis's smell (Smith et al., 2022). THC and CBD content were not compared between the categories, and no effects on people were measured. In the 41,201 THC-dominant samples with terpene results, a score of how much more samples resemble others with the same label than samples with the nearest other label (the silhouette score, from −1 to 1) averaged −0.03 for the categories, with most samples below zero, against 0.27 when samples were grouped by their most abundant terpene and 0.38 for three groups found by a clustering method in the same terpene data, which the authors expected to separate better; the category analysis also counted 12,322 samples (29.9%) that had no category as a group of their own. Strain names carried more information: for 26 of the 41 names attached to at least five growers with at least five samples each, products sold under the same name by different growers were more alike in terpene profile than names shuffled at random, 13 did not differ from chance and 2 (LSD and Durban Poison) were less alike than chance (editors' count of the significance marks in the paper's figure); even randomly paired products were fairly similar, at about 0.69 on a 0-to-1 similarity scale (read from the figure). Among 12,063 THC-dominant products with a category, Sativa products made up 30.9% of the terpinolene-rich group against 15.0% overall, yet that group was still mostly Hybrid (55.8%), and the test the paper reports for this appears to have been computed on percentages rather than counts (editors' calculation). The six laboratories' methods were not standardized, which the authors say prevents them from separating laboratory from regional differences, and the corresponding author is employed by the website that supplied the categories and strain names. In a small Dutch study, two cultivars that a seed company's website describes as Sativa-dominant (Amnesia) and Indica-dominant (White Widow), bought at ten coffee shops in four cities on two visits about two months apart (35 samples), differed in terpenes and minor cannabinoids but had similar THC (about 17% and 16% of the weight); many compounds varied by more than 25% between purchases of the same name, 3 samples had the chemistry of the other cultivar and were left out as presumed mix-ups, and of three pharmacy varieties one, bred from a variety with a large share of Sativa genes, resembled the Indica-dominant cultivar (Hazekamp & Fischedick, 2012; no statistical tests; the first author worked for the grower of the pharmacy varieties). Neither study measured how the products felt, so neither can say whether the labels predict effects. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Do indica and sativa labels tell you what's in your weed? Mostly not. In lab tests of 41,201 THC-rich flower samples from six US states, samples that a strain website calls indica, hybrid or sativa were mixed together in their terpenes, the compounds behind weed's smell: on average, a sample was about as close to another label's samples as to its own. Strain names did somewhat better: for 26 of 41 common names, products from different growers were more alike than chance, but for 13 they were not, and 2 names were less alike than chance. Sativa labels were twice as common among terpinolene-rich products, though even there most were labelled hybrid. The study compared only these smell compounds, not THC or CBD, used the website's labels rather than the packages, and measured no effects on people. A small Dutch study found that two coffee-shop strains, one described as sativa-type and one as indica-type, differed in terpenes but had similar THC, and varied a lot from purchase to purchase.
population: Dried female cannabis flower submitted by licensed growers (3,319 producers) for state compliance testing at six commercial laboratories in Alaska, California, Florida, Michigan, Oregon and Washington, December 2013 to January 2021: 89,923 samples after cleaning, 42,843 with terpene results, 41,201 THC-dominant samples with terpene results in the label analysis, and 13,401 THC-dominant products (one producer's samples under one name, averaged), 12,063 of them with a category; 41 strain names in the name analysis. Also 35 samples of two cultivars bought at ten Dutch coffee shops in four cities (purchase dates not given; paper received November 2011) and three Dutch pharmacy varieties
exposure: The Indica, Hybrid or Sativa category and the popular strain name that a consumer cannabis website's strain database attaches to each name, matched to growers' sample names by string matching and an expert dictionary of name variants (not read from packages); in the Dutch study, the name under which a sample was bought and each cultivar's Sativa or Indica background as given by a seed company's website
comparator: Samples with other categories or names; groupings built from the same terpene data (each sample's most abundant terpene; three clusters found by k-means); names shuffled at random across growers (200 repetitions); in the Dutch study, the other cultivar and three pharmacy varieties grown under controlled conditions
outcome: How closely samples sharing a label resembled each other in terpene profile (silhouette score; cosine similarity between growers' products against shuffled names; share of a name's products in its most common terpene cluster; category shares by cluster); in the Dutch study, separation of the two cultivars in a principal component analysis of 28 compounds, THC content and variation between purchases. No effects on people were measured
magnitude: Smith et al. (2022), THC-dominant samples with terpene results (n = 41,201): mean silhouette score −0.03 for the Indica/Hybrid/Sativa category (groups: Hybrid 17,616, no category 12,322, Indica 6,681, Sativa 4,582), 0.27 for the dominant terpene and 0.38 for three k-means clusters; differences |d′| = 3.49 (k-means against category), 1.83 (dominant terpene against category) and 0.54 (k-means against dominant terpene), all P < 0.0001; no intervals. Clusters: I (caryophyllene-limonene) 21,811 (52.9%), II (myrcene-pinene) 14,188 (34.4%), III (terpinolene-myrcene) 5,202 (12.6%). Strain names (41): more consistent than shuffled names for 26, no different for 13, less consistent for 2 (LSD, Durban Poison) (editors' count of the Fig 8C significance marks; the text gives one test for the majority of names, P < 0.0001, |d′| = 1.44 as printed); shuffled baseline about 0.69 cosine similarity (read from Fig 8C); Purple Punch 96% of products in one cluster against 61.8% expected under shuffling, Tangie 62.5% in its most common cluster. Category shares among 12,063 products with a category (editors' sum of the Fig 9A legend): overall Hybrid 60.6%, Indica 24.4%, Sativa 15.0%; Cluster III Hybrid 55.8%, Indica 13.3%, Sativa 30.9% (χ² 22.2, P < 0.0001 as printed); editors' calculation: the χ² formula applied to the Fig 9B percentages as if they were counts gives 22.3 for Cluster III and 1.2 and 0.6 for Clusters I and II, which the paper reports as not different. Hazekamp & Fischedick (2012): THC 167.5 mg/g (SD 21.88) in Amnesia against 159.5 (SD 26.76) in White Widow, reported as not significantly different with no test shown; myrcene 0.7 against 2.9 mg/g; terpinolene 1.9 mg/g in Amnesia, not detected in White Widow; relative standard deviation above 25% for 14 compounds as printed (editors' count of Table 1: 14 compound-and-cultivar pairs, 13 distinct compounds); 3 of 35 samples bought under one name matched the other cultivar.

risk_of_bias.note: Not rated down separately: the category result rests on 41,201 samples and is visible in the raw scatter (Fig 6A). Unstandardized methods across six laboratories and repeat submissions by the same producer add noise and dependence, and the cluster χ² and some effect sizes are unreliable (card sc_smith_2022, JBI moderate), but these weaken the secondary associations, which the statement words with their limits. The Dutch study is at high risk of bias (small unsystematic sample, post hoc exclusions, no tests, a conflict of interest; card sc_hazekamp_2012) and only qualifies the claim.

inconsistency.note: The Dutch study points the same way on variation within names, and on THC not telling its two cultivars apart; with two cultivars it cannot test the categories in general.

indirectness.note: Rated down one level: the categories tested are those a consumer website's database attaches to strain names, matched by name, not the labels printed on packages or given at sale; only terpenes were compared, not THC or CBD; the products are compliance-tested flower from six US states in 2013–2021; and nothing about effects was measured, although effects are what people usually mean by the labels.

imprecision.note: A very large sample for the category result; no intervals are printed, but the score sits near zero by a wide margin. The name results rest on 41 names and are given as counts.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one analysis of laboratory records; the cleaned data and code are stated to be public.

large_effect.note: Descriptive claim: never upgraded for a large effect (METHODS 6.3).

grade.reasoning: Descriptive analysis of product records (cross-sectional): starts low; indirectness −1 (website categories matched by name, terpenes only, US compliance-tested flower in 2013–2021, no effects), which gives very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded. 'Describes' because the claim reports how labels and chemistry line up in products, not an effect on people. The central finding, that the categories barely separate terpene profiles, is firmer than the secondary ones: the strain-name counts are the editors' count of figure marks (the paper gives one summary test, and the recount agrees with the first reader's), and the Sativa-terpinolene association rests on a test that appears to use percentages. The claim does not adopt the authors' conclusions about effects and marketing, which go beyond the chemistry measured, nor the Dutch study's estimate that 20% of coffee-shop visits gave an unreliable product, which counts presumed mix-ups the authors concede may be genuine. Status single study: the Dutch study tested two cultivars and qualifies the claim; the earlier label studies the US paper describes were not read.
